h1:
Visiting Lamphun for
the First Time + Itinerary
intro: Lamphun is one of the smallest towns in northern Thailand, but also one of the country's oldest — more than 1,300 years old. Most people drive straight past it on the way to Chiang Mai without stopping, even though the town sits just about 26 km away. If this is your first time, this guide pulls together everything worth knowing before you go: how to get there, where to go, what to eat, what to bring home — and it wraps up with a ready-to-use itinerary.

blocks.html: Lamphun was the former capital of the Hariphunchai kingdom, an ancient city that Queen Chamthewi came to rule around 1,300 years ago. Its charm is the quiet and the old-world feel that still has a pulse. The town is small enough to walk, the old temples cluster close together, and it isn't crowded with tourists the way Chiang Mai is. If you like slow towns where you can pay your respects at temples, look at old things, then sit at a café over quiet rice-field views, Lamphun hits the mark.

blocks.text: Where Lamphun is and how to get there

blocks.html: Lamphun sits right south of Chiang Mai — only about 26 km from the city center, a 30–40 minute drive. That's why most people base themselves in Chiang Mai and visit Lamphun as a day trip. But stay one night and you'll catch the old town in the evening and early morning, when most visitors never see it.

items: Private car — the most convenient. Take the Chiang Mai–Lampang superhighway, around 30–40 minutes to the town center. Parking is easy, and it's ideal if you also want to head out to Pa Sang or the cafés outside town.
Minivan / songthaew — Chiang Mai–Lamphun minivans run often and cost only a few dozen baht. They pass through Saraphi into the town center, great if you're only sightseeing within town.
Northern Line train — take the train from Chiang Mai station to Lamphun station for the atmosphere and a cheap fare, but services aren't frequent, so check the outbound and return times first.
Flying — Lamphun has no airport. You fly into Chiang Mai airport, then continue by road for about 30–40 minutes.

blocks.title: Getting around locally
blocks.html: In the town of Lamphun the sights sit very close together — easy to walk or cycle. But if you want to head to Pa Sang for the cotton weaving or the cafés outside town, it helps to have your own car or a rented motorbike, since public transport doesn't reach many spots. Taxis and Grab are also scarcer here than in Chiang Mai.
If your time is limited, hit this group first. All of these are genuine Hariphunchai-era monuments, and most are in town or just a few minutes' drive away.

items.name: Wat Phra That Hariphunchai
items.blurb: A golden chedi in the middle of town, over a thousand years old, and the year-temple for people born in the Year of the Rooster. It's the heart of the city and the first stop everyone makes in Lamphun. No entry fee.

items.name: Wat Chamthewi (Ku Kut)
items.blurb: An old temple outside the city walls. The highlight is the five-tiered, square, prasat-style chedi — a rare piece of Hariphunchai architecture, said to hold the ashes of Queen Chamthewi.

items.name: Hariphunchai National Museum
items.blurb: Right across from Wat Phra That, displaying Hariphunchai–Lanna art, votive tablets and ancient inscriptions. You can grasp the city's history in about an hour. Entry is just a few dozen baht.

items.name: Ku Chang–Ku Ma
items.blurb: Monuments on the edge of town. Ku Chang is believed to be the burial site of Queen Chamthewi's war elephant, and locals come here to make wishes regularly.

blocks.html: Add the Queen Chamthewi monument in the public park in the town center, plus an evening stroll along the conch-shell-shaped old city moat — quiet corners that photograph well and cost nothing.
Lamphun is a true northern-Thai food town — cheaper than Chiang Mai, with local dishes you rarely find elsewhere. Starting the morning with something local before you head out is just right.

items: Khanom jeen nam ngiao — a northern breakfast favorite. The nam ngiao broth has a gentle sourness, eaten with crispy pork rinds and fresh vegetables. Bowls start at a few dozen baht.
Stewed pork noodles with longan — a local specialty that puts actual longan in the broth for a rounded sweetness. It sounds odd but it's moreish, and you'll find it around town.
Khao soi and northern dishes — chicken khao soi, nam phrik ong, nam phrik num, sai ua — available at northern-Thai restaurants all over town.
Rice-field-view cafés — there are several cafés out in the fields outside town. Sipping coffee over green paddies is a rest stop the younger crowd loves.

blocks.text: What to bring home from Lamphun

blocks.html: Lamphun has two genuinely distinctive things to bring home. Buy them straight from the source and you get a good price plus the story behind them.

items.name: Ban Don Luang hand-woven cotton
items.blurb: The most famous cotton-weaving community in Lamphun, in Pa Sang district about 14 km from town. You'll find sarongs, scarves and cotton clothing made by the weavers themselves, at better prices than the malls.

items.name: Longan and longan products
items.blurb: Lamphun is one of Thailand's top longan provinces. From July–August there's cheap fresh longan straight from the orchards; out of season, dried longan and longan juice work as a gift year-round.

blocks.text: The plan — a ready-to-use Lamphun itinerary

blocks.html: Here are two versions. Got half a day to a full day? Use the first plan and cover the in-town highlights. Staying a night? Add a second day out to Pa Sang for the cotton weaving and cafés. Adjust the timing to suit you.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Cover the old Hariphunchai city in one day

items.note: Start the morning with a local northern dish in town and fuel up before you head out. A few dozen baht per bowl.
The golden chedi in the middle of town. Walk around the chedi, the old bell and the lion gate. No entry fee. Dress modestly — shoulders and knees covered. Open roughly 06:00–18:00.
Right across from Wat Phra That — just cross the road. See Hariphunchai art and ancient inscriptions. Entry is a few dozen baht and it takes about 45 minutes.

items.activity: Lunch — stewed pork noodles with longan
items.note: Try the local dish with longan in the broth, or a northern-Thai restaurant near Wat Phra That works too.
A few minutes' drive outside the city walls. See the five-tiered, square, prasat-style chedi — true Hariphunchai architecture that became the model for Lanna chedis.

items.activity: Ku Chang–Ku Ma + Queen Chamthewi monument
items.note: Stop at the Ku Chang monument where locals come to make wishes, then continue to the Queen Chamthewi monument in the town-center public park.

items.activity: Stroll along the old city moat
items.note: In the softer light, walk along the conch-shell-shaped moat and catch the little temples along the way. A calm, quiet atmosphere.
Close the day with northern food or a place in town. If you're doing it as a day trip, it's about a 30–40 minute drive back to Chiang Mai.
Eat in town, pack up, then head out to Pa Sang district — about 14 km, roughly 20 minutes.

items.activity: Ban Don Luang, Pa Sang — cotton-weaving village
items.note: Walk around the looms, chat with the weavers, and pick out sarongs, scarves and cotton clothing made by hand — a souvenir that comes with a story.
Ban Don Luang has several fabric shops in a row. Compare patterns and prices before you buy. Late in the year there's often a community cotton fair.
Find a made-to-order spot or a local restaurant in the district town. Eat up before the café stop.
Wrap up the trip at a café out in the fields around the Lamphun industrial estate or outside town. Sip coffee over green paddies — a rest stop before you head back.

items.activity: Buy longan gifts, then head back
items.note: Stop for dried longan, longan juice or a little more cotton fabric before driving back to Chiang Mai or on to your next stop.

items: Nov–Feb (cool season) — the best time. Cool, comfortable weather lets you do temples, the old town and cafés all day without the heat.
Jul–Aug (longan season) — eat cheap fresh longan straight from the orchards, a charm unique to Lamphun, and the paddies are a beautiful green.
Aug–Sep (rainy season) — the paddies are at their greenest, perfect for rice-field cafés, but build in extra time for the rain.
Mar–Apr — hot, with some haze at times, like much of northern Thailand. If you come then, focus on early-morning and evening sightseeing for more comfort.

blocks.html: Lamphun really can be done cheaply — most temples are free to enter and food is cheap. The main variable is how much cotton fabric and longan you buy to take home.

items: Day trip from Chiang Mai — fuel/transport, food and entry fees, around 500–1,000 THB total.
One night (2 days) — in-town accommodation around 600–1,500 THB, food and cafés around 500–900 THB.
Comfortable overnight total — roughly 1,800–3,500 THB per person, not counting cotton fabric and longan souvenirs.

blocks.title: Pairs well with Chiang Mai
blocks.html: On a first visit many people do Lamphun as a day trip from Chiang Mai, which is easy because it's so close. But stay one night and you get the old-town atmosphere in the evening and early morning, which is much quieter — worth the overnight if you have the time.

blocks.text: Things to know before you go

items: Temple dress code — Wat Phra That Hariphunchai and Wat Chamthewi are sacred temples. Dress modestly, shoulders and knees covered. Some spots lend out cover-ups.
Shops close early — Lamphun is a small town and many restaurants and cafés close in the evening, so nights are quiet. Plan dinner early.
Carry cash — many local shops and weaving communities take mainly cash, so it's easier to keep some on you.
Mornings have the edge — temples and the museum open early, the weather's good and there are fewer people for better photos. Start early and you'll cover everything without rushing.

faq.q: How many days do I need on a first visit to Lamphun?
faq.a: If you're short on time, it works easily as a day trip from Chiang Mai — they're only about 26 km apart, a 30–40 minute drive, and you can cover the in-town highlights in one day. But if you want the old-town atmosphere in the evening and morning, stay one night and add a second day out to Pa Sang for the cotton weaving and a rice-field café.

faq.q: What is there to do in Lamphun?
faq.a: The highlights are Wat Phra That Hariphunchai, Wat Chamthewi (Ku Kut), the Hariphunchai National Museum, Ku Chang–Ku Ma, the Queen Chamthewi monument, walking the old town along the moat, and the Ban Don Luang cotton-weaving village in Pa Sang district — plus the rice-field-view cafés outside town.

faq.q: How do I get from Chiang Mai to Lamphun?
faq.a: Driving your own car is the most convenient — take the superhighway about 26 km, a 30–40 minute drive. Or take a Chiang Mai–Lamphun minivan, which runs often and costs only a few dozen baht. The Northern Line train to Lamphun station has nice atmosphere but services aren't frequent, so check the times first.

faq.q: Do I need my own car to visit Lamphun?
faq.a: In town you can walk or cycle since the sights are close together. But to reach Pa Sang for the cotton weaving or the cafés outside town, it helps to have your own car or a rented motorbike, since public transport doesn't reach many spots and Grab is scarcer than in Chiang Mai.

faq.q: What's the best souvenir to buy in Lamphun?
faq.a: Hand-woven cotton from Ban Don Luang in Pa Sang district is the most famous souvenir — sarongs, scarves and cotton clothing — along with longan products like dried longan or longan juice, since Lamphun is one of Thailand's top longan provinces.
